03 · Case study · Real-time AI

In voice systems, latency is product quality.

A conversational voice application: speech recognition, LLM inference, and speech synthesis, orchestrated asynchronously over WebSockets. Built to feel like talking to a person, monitored like infrastructure.

Context

Three slow operations in sequence — hear, think, speak — with a human waiting on the other end. Run them one after another and the conversation feels broken. The product only works if the whole pipeline fits inside a latency budget a person finds natural.

In a real-time system, a slow stage is a product defect.

Architecture

Decision

The pipeline runs asynchronously over WebSockets: recognition, inference, and synthesis overlap instead of waiting on each other. Each stage is monitored like infrastructure — in a real-time system, a slow stage is a product defect.

Constraint

No stage could be allowed to stall the conversation, and no latency figure could be assumed — the design had to overlap work and monitor every stage, without inventing targets that didn't exist.

Result

A voice system that holds a natural conversation, with latency treated as a feature of the product rather than a number on a dashboard.

Run them one after another and the conversation feels broken.

Lessons

  1. In voice, every unnecessary pause makes the product feel broken.
  2. Async overlap is a design decision, not an optimization.
  3. Monitor real-time stages like infrastructure, because they are.

Stack

Deepgram · Groq · ElevenLabs · Twilio · FastAPI
